title: The Threshing Floor and the Gate

date.label: Undated Ruth narrative
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: Ruth 3:1–4:17 is one continuous resolution arc: a single night at the threshing floor (ch. 3) fulfilled "this day" at the gate (4:1–12), with marriage and birth following without a time or scene break (4:13–17).
claims.evidence: Read record (ruth-read-ch03-04.md, boundary table); Mechon Mamre Ruth 3 (18 vv.) and Ruth 4 (22 vv.) opened live; K&D introduction to Ruth 3 and Ruth 4.

claims.claim: *Manoach* ("rest") in 3:1 means a peaceful, well-secured condition — a settled life under a husband's guardian care — the same word as *menuchah* in 1:9.
claims.evidence: K&D on Ruth 3:1–5, citing Rosenmüller.

claims.claim: Boaz winnowed barley at night on an open-air threshing floor — a hard, level, often circular surface outside the town, worked in the evening breeze — and slept there at the end of the grain heap to guard the crop.
claims.evidence: K&D on Ruth 3:1–5 (Robinson's floor description; evening wind) and 3:6–7; BiblicalTraining "Threshing Floor" (location, construction, winnowing, night guarding).

claims.claim: Winnowing used the evening wind to separate grain from chaff, tossed with fork and shovel; barley was the spring crop, wheat following weeks later.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining "Threshing Floor" (winnowing and storing; harvest timetable).

claims.claim: "Spread thy skirt over thine handmaid" (*kanaf*, literally "wing") is a claim to marriage, not merely a request for shelter: the figure is the corner of the covering a man spreads over his wife, as in Ezek 16:8.
claims.evidence: K&D on Ruth 3:9 (Deut 22:30 Heb. 23:1; Ezek 16:8); answered by 2:12 ("under whose wings").

claims.claim: Ruth is called *eshet chayil* ("a virtuous woman," literally a woman of strength/valor); the phrase occurs only three times in the Old Testament (Ruth 3:11; Prov 12:4; Prov 31:10).
claims.evidence: K&D on Ruth 3:10–14 ("virtuous woman," known to "the whole gate of my people"); three-occurrence count verified in CBE International (read in full 2026-11-24).

claims.claim: Boaz measured six measures of barley into Ruth's shawl (*mitpachat*); the unit of measure is not stated in the text, and the Targum's "six seahs = two ephahs" is incorrect, since Ruth could not have carried that much.
claims.evidence: K&D on Ruth 3:15 (Targum/Rabbins rejected; measure not given).

claims.claim: The gate — the open space before the city gate — was the forum where the city's public affairs were discussed; Boaz's "going up" to it is the place of justice as an ideal eminence, not a topographical climb.
claims.evidence: K&D on Ruth 4:1 (cf. Deut 17:8).

claims.claim: Boaz took ten men of the elders of the city as witnesses.
claims.evidence: Mechon Mamre Ruth 4:2 (live).

claims.claim: The text states the number but gives no reason for it, and no source in this dossier explains why ten.
claims.evidence: Ruth 4:2 gives the number with no reason stated; no explanation found in K&D or elsewhere consulted.

claims.claim: The nearer kinsman is unnamed — Hebrew *peloni almoni*, "such a one," a person whose name is unknown or not thought worth mentioning.
claims.evidence: K&D on Ruth 4:1 (cf. 1 Sam 21:3; 2 Kgs 6:8).

claims.claim: Naomi had sold Elimelech's field from want; the sale was of yearly produce until the Jubilee, not of the land itself; the widow remained in possession during her life, and the field would pass to the nearest relations.
claims.evidence: K&D on Ruth 4:2–5 (Lev 25:10, 13–16, 24–28; Num 27:8–11); Lev 25 framework in clm-lev-jc-001–003.

claims.claim: The nearer kinsman refused because redeeming plus marrying Ruth would mar his own inheritance: the redeemed field would pass to the son born through Ruth, so his outlay would benefit another line.
claims.evidence: K&D on Ruth 4:6–13 (economic reading of "lest I mar mine own inheritance").

claims.claim: In the former custom, the man surrendering a right drew off his own shoe and gave it to his neighbour; in Ruth 4:8 the refusing kinsman gives his shoe to Boaz, as a token transferring a possession or right of ownership (grounded in taking possession by treading the soil).
claims.evidence: Mechon Mamre Ruth 4:7–8 (live); K&D on Ruth 4:7–8 (shoe as transfer symbol; cf. Deut 25:9 discussion).

claims.claim: The sandal exchange is a conveyancing gesture for redemption and exchange, NOT the *halitzah* rite of Deut 25:7–10: the man acts himself, no widow acts, there is no spitting, and the act confirms a transfer rather than shaming a refusal.
claims.evidence: K&D on Ruth 4:7–8; narrator's gloss "concerning redeeming and concerning changing"; published clm-deu-06-069 (probable).

claims.claim: *Ga'al* (H1350) means "redeem, act as kinsman": (a) taking a kinsman's widow (Ruth 3:13); (b) redeeming from bondage (Lev 25:48–49); (c) redeeming a field (Lev 25:26, 33; Ruth 4:4, 6); (d) *go'el hadam*, avenger of blood (Num 35:19; Deut 19:6); and (e) with God as subject, redeeming Israel from bondage and exile.
claims.evidence: BDB H1350 entry read directly (bibliaparalela mirror of BDB).

claims.claim: Ruth 4 is redemption by a *go'el* under a traditional custom that attached a widow-marriage obligation to the redemption of the land; it is NOT a levirate marriage contracted under Deut 25:5–10, which bound only a brother.
claims.evidence: K&D introduction to Ruth 3 ("these two institutions are not connected together in the Mosaic law" but custom joined them); published clm-deu-06-069 and clm-deu-06-076 (probable).

claims.claim: The gate blessing wishes Ruth like Rachel and Leah, "which two did build the house of Israel," and Boaz to "do worthily in Ephrath" — *'aseh chayil* meaning to get power by begetting and training worthy sons and daughters, not to get wealth — and to be famous in Bethlehem.
The blessing "let thy house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore unto Judah" invokes Gen 38; Perez is the ancestor from whom Boaz's line descends (Ruth 4:18; 1 Chr 2:5).
claims.evidence: K&D on Ruth 4:12; Mechon Mamre Gen 38 (30 vv., opened live).

claims.claim: Boaz took Ruth, the LORD gave her conception, and she bore a son; the women call the child Naomi's *go'el* and say he will restore her life and nourish her old age; Naomi takes him to her bosom and becomes his nurse; the neighbour women name him Obed, "a son is born to Naomi," and he is the father of Jesse, the father of David.
claims.evidence: Mechon Mamre Ruth 4:13–17 (live); K&D on Ruth 4:13–17 (Obed = "the serving one," not "servant of Jehovah").

claims.claim: A real tension exists between the Deut 23:3 exclusion of Ammonites and Moabites from the assembly of the LORD "for ever" and Ruth the Moabitess being taken as wife and bearing a son in Israel. No character in Ruth raises the exclusion, and the narrator offers no gloss resolving it.
claims.evidence: Mechon Mamre Deut 23 (Heb. v. 4 = Eng. v. 3, opened live); Mechon Mamre Ruth 4:5, 10, 13 (live); published conn-deu-06-023 ("noted, not resolved").

claims.claim: Any resolution of the tension between the Deut 23:3 exclusion and Ruth the Moabitess being taken as wife and bearing a son in Israel — the four candidate readings set out in §8.4.
claims.evidence: No resolution is adopted in this dossier; the four candidate readings are set out in §8.4 (see RCL-03-021, RCL-03-022); published conn-deu-06-023 ("noted, not resolved").

claims.claim: Candidate reading (a): the exclusion applies to male Ammonites/Moabites only, so a Moabite woman could marry into Israel — the rabbinic reading (Mishnah *Yebamot* 8:3; b. *Yebamot* 77a), argued from the stated reason (bread and water; hiring Balaam) as men's acts.
claims.evidence: Levin (Torah.org) on Ketubot 7a / Yebamot 77b and the reason-based argument; Wright (TheTorah.com) on Mishnah Yebamot 8:3. Talmud not read directly.

claims.claim: Candidate reading (c): the narrative itself resolves the exclusion — Ruth's oath, refuge, public character, the elders' blessing, and the LORD giving her conception amount to a narrative verdict of acceptance; Braulik's form: Ruth as intra-biblical critique/homily on Deut 23–25.
claims.evidence: Mechon Mamre Ruth 4:10–13 read in full (Hebrew + JPS English): the elders' blessing at 4:11, the label's absence at 4:13, and the LORD giving conception. Braulik, abstract + excerpts (full article not read directly); Wright on the community's welcome (Ruth 4:11) and the label dropping at 4:13.

claims.claim: ANE parallels for the sandal conveyance (Alalakh AT 456; Nuzi HSS 19, 67; Hittite/Middle Assyrian footwear material) are asserted in web summaries but were NOT independently verified in this dossier; no claim about them is made.
claims.evidence: No primary edition or scholarly publication opened; no registry source. See §5.

claims.claim: Identifying a threshing floor archaeologically is difficult: an Iron Age layered feature at Tel Megiddo previously assumed to be a threshing floor was re-identified as a single-household trash heap, and similar identifications should be re-evaluated.
claims.evidence: Shahack-Gross, Gafri & Finkelstein, Journal of Field Archaeology 34(2), 171–184 (2009), read in full via the freely accessible ResearchGate publication page, 2026-11-23 (abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion, references).

claims.claim: "Ephrath" in the blessing ("do thou worthily in Ephrath") is not settled as identical with Bethlehem: the Ephrath gloss is debated, and "that is Bethlehem" may be a later gloss.
claims.evidence: Published clm-ij-063 (debated; Skinner); K&D on Ruth 4:11 treats Ephrath/Bethlehem as the blessing's own pairing without deciding identity.

connections.note: Boaz's blessing speaks of refuge under the LORD's wings; the threshing-floor scene answers it when Ruth asks Boaz to spread his own wing over her.
Naomi first names Boaz as a near kinsman with the right of redemption, the thread the threshing-floor night and the gate scene carry to its end.
Naomi's farewell prayer that her daughters-in-law find rest in a husband's house is the wish the threshing-floor plan sets out to fulfil.
The levirate statute and its refusal rite stand behind the gate procedure, but the marriage in Ruth is redemption by a kinsman, not a marriage under this statute.
The land belongs to the LORD and a kinsman redeems what poverty forced a relative to sell; this is the law behind the field of Elimelech at the gate.
The same kinsman-redeemer law covers redeeming a relative from bondage, showing the breadth of the redeemer's duty beyond land alone.
The law barring Ammonites and Moabites from the assembly, with its stated reasons, stands in open tension with Ruth the Moabitess being taken as wife; the tension is carried here, not settled.

After the exile the same law is read aloud and applied to separate from all foreign descent — the strict reading against which Ruth's welcome stands out, which sharpens the tension without resolving it.
Judah and Tamar give the pre-Mosaic instance of raising up a name for the dead, and the gate blessing itself names Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah.
Lot's daughters bear Moab and Ben-ammi, the origin of the people Ruth comes from; the exclusion's stated reason is not this origin but inhospitality and Balaam.
Balak of Moab sends for Balaam to curse Israel, the hiring the exclusion in Deuteronomy gives as its second reason.
Wrongdoing is judged at the gates with witnesses, the same public gate setting where Boaz settles the redemption.
A case is brought to the elders at the gate, the established pattern for the elders Boaz gathers as witnesses.
A dispute is heard before the elders at the gate, another instance of the gate as the town's court.
The LORD spreads his skirt over Jerusalem and takes her as wife, the closest parallel to Ruth's request for Boaz to spread his skirt over her.
A woman of strength is her husband's crown, the same phrase Boaz uses of Ruth before the whole town.
The poem of the woman of strength gives the fullest portrait of the phrase Boaz applies to Ruth.
Gideon threshes wheat hidden in a winepress for fear of Midian, the contrast case showing threshing normally happened on the open floor.
David buys Araunah's threshing floor and builds an altar there, the best-known threshing floor in the Bible and a sign of how such open places could change use.
Rachel dies on the way to Ephrath, the place-name behind the blessing's mention of Ephrath; whether Ephrath is Bethlehem is debated.
The threshing floor of Atad serves as a gathering and mourning place, showing floors were large open spaces used for more than threshing.
The order of inheritance when a man dies without sons is the law behind who held Elimelech's field and who could redeem it.
Every place the sole of the foot treads is given as possession, the image behind the shoe as a token of transferred land-right.
The barren woman bears seven sons, the picture of full blessing behind the women's words that Ruth is better to Naomi than seven sons.
Perez's line is listed there, the genealogy the gate blessing and the book's ending both point toward.
The genealogy of Perez closes the book from Perez to David; it is its own unit, carried by the next category, and is linked here only as the story's forward edge.
